title: Numbness on the Medical Take: An Atypical Presentation of Guillain‐Barre Syndrome With Unilateral Paraesthesia and Rapid Progression to Bulbar Palsy: A Case Report
case_prompt:
A 73-year-old woman presented with a 12-hour history of left-sided hand and foot paresthesia and reduced mobility. She had awoken with these symptoms and was initially triaged as a stroke thrombolysis call but was ineligible for thrombolysis because the symptoms began on awakening. Two weeks earlier she had experienced cough, fever, and myalgias that resolved 2–3 days before presentation. Her medical history included resected colon adenocarcinoma (2015), cholecystectomy, cervical canal stenosis, and longstanding right foot drop; she was also under investigation for chronic right arm weakness. Medications (unchanged in the past month) were citalopram, solifenacin, amlodipine, atorvastatin, and propranolol.

On examination, sensation was decreased in the left hand to the level of the wrist and in both forefeet, in a nondermatomal distribution. There was no new motor weakness; muscle tone and deep-tendon reflexes were normal in all four limbs. Vital signs were within normal limits. Initial CT of the brain with CT angiography showed no hemorrhage, stroke, or large-vessel occlusion. Routine blood tests, including inflammatory markers, electrolytes, renal function, B12, folate, and thyroid-stimulating hormone, were all within reference ranges. A provisional diagnosis of atypical stroke was made, and plans were made for discharge on clopidogrel with outpatient TIA clinic follow-up and MRI brain. However, because she was unable to mobilize independently despite normal motor strength and reflexes, she was admitted for further investigation and support.
diagnostic_reasoning:
1. Stroke or TIA considered — “A provisional diagnosis of atypical stroke was considered due to the acuity of onset of her symptoms and a plan was made to discharge with clopidogrel for outpatient TIA…”
2. Typical GBS thought unlikely initially — “GBS typically presents with motor symptoms, most commonly an ascending, symmetrical weakness and reduced or absent reflexes.”
3. Pure sensory GBS questioned — “Pure sensory GBS (sensory deficits without motor involvement throughout the disease course) is controversial with only a small number of reported cases… which would not satisfy current diagnostic criteria for GBS.”
4. Miller Fisher syndrome excluded — “It was not felt to be MFS due to the absence of ophthalmoplegia or ataxia.”
5. Bickerstaff brainstem encephalitis excluded — “It was not felt to be BBE due to the absence of impaired consciousness or ophthalmoplegia typical of BBE.”
6. Pharyngeal cervical-brachial variant excluded — “It was not felt to be PCB due to the presence of lower limb weakness in addition to bulbar weakness.”
